engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Middlegame: Piece Coordination
chess.body: Good chess is about all your pieces working together. Ask: which of my pieces is worst placed? Improve it. A knight on the rim is dim (a1, h1 etc). A bishop blocked by its own pawns is a 'tall pawn.' Rooks need open files. Queen needs safety. Coordinate: every piece pointing at the same sector = overwhelming attack.

wisdom.title: Regulate Yourself First
wisdom.body: You cannot be a calm parent if you're running on stress, sleep debt, and financial anxiety. Your regulation is their regulation — babies co-regulate with caregivers. Deep breath before you pick her up. Shoulders down. Slow exhale. Your nervous system sets the tone for the room.

book.author: Clayton Christensen
book.chapter: Why Great Companies Fail at Exactly the Right Moment
book.lesson: Christensen's paradox: the best-managed companies, doing everything right — listening to customers, investing in quality, maximising margins — are the most vulnerable to disruption. Disruptive technologies start at the bottom of the market (cheaper, simpler, worse performance) serving customers who don't exist yet. They improve over time until they're good enough for mainstream customers. By then, it's too late for incumbents to respond. Nokia had better technology than Apple in 2007. Blockbuster had better retail locations than Netflix. They failed not despite their excellence but because of it — their success made them unable to cannibalise themselves.
book.key_quote: Excellence in executing today's business model can blind you to the business model that will replace it.
book.action: Ask about your industry: what is the simpler, cheaper, 'worse' solution that currently serves the bottom of the market? Could it eventually serve everyone?
crux: Well-managed companies fail precisely by doing what good management prescribes.
Sustaining innovations improve products for existing customers. Incumbents win these reliably.
Disruptive innovations start worse on the metrics incumbents value, and win anyway.
Disruption enters at the low end or in a new market, where incumbent margins look unattractive.
Listening closely to your best customers pushes you away from disruptive bets. Rationally.
Resource dependence: customers and investors, not managers, effectively allocate the resources.
Small markets cannot solve the growth needs of large companies, so large companies skip them.
Technology supply often outruns demand — products overshoot what users need, opening the low end.
The basis of competition shifts over time: function → reliability → convenience → price.
You cannot analyse markets that do not yet exist. Discovery-driven planning, not forecasting.
Disruption must be housed in an independent organisation small enough to be excited by a small win.
Failure early and cheaply is the plan, because the first strategy will be wrong.
learnings: Doing everything right is not protection when the game changes underneath.
The customers who fund you today are the reason you miss tomorrow.
A market too small to matter now is the only place disruption can start.
Cost structure determines which opportunities look attractive. It is destiny.
examples: Disk drives: every generational shift from 14-inch to 1.8-inch killed the leader, though each new size was initially worse on capacity.
Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975 and could not commit to it without cannibalising film margins.
Mini-mills started with low-grade rebar that integrated steel mills were happy to abandon, then moved up until they took the whole market.
adapt: A free Telegram bot is the low-end disruption of paid research. That is the position to hold, not apologise for.
Codex at $47 looks unattractive next to consulting rates. That is exactly why it has room.
Don't let existing dashboard users dictate the roadmap if the measured edge points elsewhere.
Keep experiments in separate ledgers — the APEX poly engine on its own books, so a small bet stays a small bet.

minimalism.title: The Empty Surface
minimalism.body: Keep one surface in your home completely empty. A desk, a counter, a shelf. It becomes a visual reference point — the moment things start accumulating elsewhere, you notice.
minimalism.action: Clear one surface fully. Keep it clear for a week.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Dress One Notch Above The Room
etiquette.body: Not two — two reads as trying. One notch signals you took the occasion seriously. In the Gulf, conservative beats fashionable in every professional setting.
etiquette.action: Check tomorrow's outfit against the room you will be in.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Silence Is A Position
stillness.body: You are not required to have an opinion on everything you encounter. 'I don't know enough about that' is a complete and unusually strong answer.
stillness.action: Decline to have an opinion on one thing today.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Inversion
model.body: Solve the problem backwards. Instead of 'how do I succeed?', ask 'how would I guarantee failure?' — then avoid that. The failure list is concrete and short; the success list is vague and infinite.
model.action: Invert your biggest current goal. Write the three surest ways to fail it.
model.label: Mental Model

arabic.use: Universal. Starting a meeting, leaving a room, urging someone along.
arabic.label: Arabic

drill.title: Name The Assumption
drill.body: Every model rests on two or three assumptions doing all the work. Find them. The rest is arithmetic and does not deserve your review time.
drill.action: Find the two assumptions carrying your current model.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Strength Is Longevity, Not Vanity
health.body: Muscle mass and grip strength both independently predict lifespan. After 30 you lose 3–8% of muscle per decade unless you resist it, and the decline accelerates. Sarcopenia is what puts people in care homes.
health.action: Two sets of a compound lift. Squat, hinge, push, or pull.
health.label: Health

quote.name: Tim Ferriss
quote.quote: Focus on being productive instead of busy.

lesson.lesson: It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop.

case.title: Tesla: Make the Most Expensive Car First
case.story: Tesla launched with a $100K Roadster. Then $70K Model S. Then $35K Model 3. They used premium pricing to fund mass-market production.
case.lesson: Start expensive to build the brand, fund R&D, and attract early adopters. Then scale down. Starting cheap makes it hard to go premium.

fpna.title: Sensitivity Analysis
fpna.body: Which assumption, if wrong, blows up your model? Identify it. Test it. Present the range.

cfo.title: CFO Step 1: Strategy + Finance
cfo.body: CFOs translate business strategy into financial reality. They ask: what's the ROI, what's the IRR, what's the payback period? Practice building business cases. Every investment decision has a financial model behind it.

money_hack.title: Index Funds over Active
money_hack.body: 85% of large-cap active funds underperform Nifty over 10 years. Index at 0.1% expense ratio.

dubai.title: What the counter-offer is really for
dubai.body: First offers in the Gulf come in 10–15% below the band because everybody counters. Not countering does not read as humble; it reads as someone who did not check.
dubai.targets: Counter once, with a number and a reason. Then stop.
dubai.action: "Based on the band for this role and my IFRS 16 experience, I was targeting AED X."

desk.productivity: Weekly review: 15 min every Sunday. What worked, what's next week's #1.

father.title: Take a photo of the ordinary
father.do: Photograph something unremarkable — her on the floor, mid-task — rather than a milestone.
father.why: You will have hundreds of milestone photos and almost none of the texture of daily life at seven months, which is what you will actually want later.

father.title: Say goodbye properly
father.do: Never slip out unseen. Say you are leaving, say you will be back, then go — even if she cries.
father.why: Disappearing without warning teaches vigilance. A predictable goodbye, repeated, teaches that departures end in returns. The crying is not the failure; it is the process.

life_wisdom.teaching: The endless wanting that survives every acquisition. Jain and Buddhist thought agree closely here — the object changes, the wanting does not.
life_wisdom.apply: Notice the next thing you tell yourself you will be satisfied after getting. Write it down. Check in six months whether the satisfaction arrived.

life_wisdom.teaching: The second element of the path, sitting between right view and right speech — the resolve that shapes what follows.
life_wisdom.apply: Before a difficult conversation, name your intention in one sentence. If it is 'to be proved right', the conversation will fail regardless of your evidence.

speaking.title: Explain it to a seven-year-old
speaking.drill: Explain IFRS 16 or working capital with no jargon, in under 40 seconds, out loud.
speaking.why: The constraint exposes whether you understand it or have memorised it.

interview_tech.q: Online returns are 30% versus 8% in store. How does that change unit economics?
interview_tech.a: It can invert them. Model the full return cost: outbound delivery, return shipping, inspection labour, repackaging, markdown on anything not resaleable as new, and the working capital locked in goods in transit. At 30% returns a nominally profitable online order can land negative. Fixes: better size guidance and imagery to cut the cause; charge for returns where the market allows; route returns to stores so the item re-enters saleable stock nearest demand. Report online contribution after returns, never before.

interview_tech.q: How would you hedge FX exposure for a retailer buying in USD and selling in MYR?
interview_tech.a: First separate transaction exposure (committed purchase orders) from translation exposure (consolidating a foreign subsidiary). Hedge transaction exposure with forwards matched to the payment dates on the buying calendar — typically rolling 6–12 months, hedging a declining percentage the further out you go. Do not hedge translation exposure with derivatives; it is an accounting effect, not a cash one. State the policy in a treasury mandate with limits, so hedging never becomes speculation with a different name.

interview_soft.q: How do you give feedback to someone more senior than you?
interview_soft.a: Ask permission, be specific, and stay on observable behaviour and its effect. 'Can I give you a reaction to how the numbers landed in that meeting? When the forecast changed without the bridge, the room stopped trusting the rest of the pack.' No adjectives about them, one concrete instance, and a suggestion. Then stop talking. Most people either avoid this entirely or overcorrect into confrontation.

interview_soft.q: How do you influence people who do not report to you?
interview_soft.a: Retail finance is almost entirely this — Buying, Operations and Retail Heads do not report to you. The answer is currency: work out what each function is measured on and frame your ask in their terms. A buyer cares about sell-through and margin, not about your working capital target — so bring them the SKU-level analysis showing which lines tie up cash without turning. Give people the analysis they cannot build themselves, and influence follows. Name a specific instance and the outcome.
